title: The Mythology of Conscious AI
lede: Neuroscientist Anil Seth's prize-winning Noema essay argues that consciousness probably depends on being alive rather than on computation, and that making AI which even seems conscious is a mistake.

points: Seth separates intelligence, which is about doing, from consciousness, which is about there being something it is like to be a system.
He traces the urge to see minds in AI to three biases: anthropocentrism, human exceptionalism and anthropomorphism.
Language makes LLMs unusually persuasive; nobody calls AlphaFold conscious, though it is built from similar parts.
He suggests saying models confabulate rather than hallucinate, since hallucination implies experience.
Believing AI feels things has costs either way: exploited vulnerabilities, distorted ethics, and machines granted rights we cannot switch off.

points.text: Many commenters say the debate is premature, since nobody can define consciousness or verify it from the outside.
Commenters split on substrate; some say ruling out silicon consciousness is hasty when no one knows what causes it in brains.
One commenter calls the life-versus-computation framing a false dichotomy and says Seth's arguments have been rebutted many times.
Another thread asks why believers in conscious agents skip the ethics: if a swarm is conscious, putting it to work looks like slavery.
